newsitem.title: UK: Ford raises strike spectre for UK's Labour party.
newsitem.headline: Ford raises strike spectre for UK's Labour party.

text.p: The decision by U.S. car giant Ford to slash jobs at its Halewood plant in northwest England is a double-edged sword for Britain's opposition Labour party.
In the run-up to an election it is tipped to win, Labour cannot afford to be linked once again in voters' minds with union unrest and picket-lines.
According to the Labour party the 1,300 job losses are a clear result of the Conservative government's steady reduction of workers' rights.
Seizing on a comment of "You can't win them all" by finance minister Kenneth Clarke, Labour has rammed home its message that "Conservative rule means job insecurity".
But behind the statements lies fear -- fear that Labour could once more become inextricably linked in voters' minds with militant unions and angry strikers.
With less than four months to an election, Labour is riding high in polls, in sight of power for the first time in 18 years.

After a painful odyssey from the left to the centre ground under leader Tony Blair, Labour appears to have neutralised Conservative charges it would be spendthrift in government, seen as a key reason for its defeat at the 1992 election.
But the prospect of strikes -- workers at Ford's 20 plants in Britain will hold meetings this week to decide their strategy -- raises bitter memories of the last time it held power.

In 1979, Prime Minister James Callaghan was brought down after a wave of public sector strikes which left rubbish rotting in the streets and the dead unburied -- a period dubbed "the Winter of Discontent".
Public anger at the strikes laid the ground for Conservative premier Margaret Thatcher to launch her campaign to curb the powers of the unions.
In 1984 came the crucial power struggle, when union leader Arthur Scargill took his miners out on strike to protest Thatcher's efforts to close uneconomic coal pits.

Despite unhappiness at Scargill's decision to bring out his members without a ballot, Labour leader Neil Kinnock -- himself a member of parliament for a mining area -- was still too close to the unions to be able to distance himself from the dispute.
Kinnock and the Labour party were compromised and neither supported the strike nor condemned picket line violence.
Unions -- not just the miners' -- were seriously weakened by Scargill's eventual defeat after one year on strike and Thatcher's "victory" helped her win an election in 1987.
New Labour, as Blair calls his overhauled party, has learnt the lesson. Last September, newspapers were told unions would get "no favours" under a Blair administration.
Labour insiders involved in employment policy believe the Ford dispute -- which crucially is in the private rather than the public sector -- will itself not shift opinion.
Indeed, they believe it could strengthen their argument that the country needs partnership between government, industry and workers in the place of confrontation.
It also, they believe, neutralises Conservative arguments againt the Social Chapter standardising worker protection across the European Union -- which Major has refused to sign.
It was Britain's failure to sign which made Ford choose to shut its British plant rather than its German plant, which would have required months of consultation, the Labour sources said.
But nervousness remains, and is driving opposition policy.
After bitter tussles, the party originally created by the unions 96 years ago to win working men and women a voice in parliament has cut the unions' influence over policy.
But Blair's biggest nightmare is of taking office only to find himself facing public sector workers demanding big pay rises they have been denied under the Conservatives.
Blair announced plans for his own "no strike" deals with public sector unions, although he has since backed off after bitter protests from within his party.
Blair is banking on cooperation from unions desperate to see Labour in power, holding back the threat of new curbs as an ultimate sanction if relations break down once he is in office.
